scenes.visual: Open-plan room vs building of walled offices
scenes.narration: Two cellular floor plans. A prokaryote — a bacterium — is an open plan: no internal membranes, no true nucleus, everything happening in one room. A eukaryote — your cells — is a building of walled offices: a membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, each doing one job. The banner says it: compartments enable specialization. That single architectural difference is the reason your cells can do things bacteria cannot.

scenes.visual: Bilayer schematic with channel and receptor
scenes.narration: The plasma membrane is the cell's outer wall, and it's a phospholipid bilayer. Hydrophilic heads face the water on both sides; the hydrophobic core in the middle blocks most molecules from crossing. That makes the membrane a selective barrier — impermeable on its own, but studded with proteins that choose what passes. Channel proteins open passages for specific ions; receptor proteins receive signals from outside. The membrane decides what gets in and what stays out.
scenes.slideTitle: The plasma membrane: a selective barrier

scenes.narration: Two ways the cell moves cargo across that barrier, and a way we proved it. On the left, a clinical correlate: in familial hypercholesterolemia, broken LDL-receptor endocytosis leaves cholesterol piling up in the arteries — endocytosis brings material in. On the right, the experiment that mapped the path out: George Palade's pulse-chase. Tag fresh protein with a brief radioactive pulse, chase with unlabeled, and watch the labeled cohort travel from rough ER to Golgi to secretion in real time. That's how we know the secretory pathway is real.

Here's the chapter's whole argument in one disease. The lysosome is the cell's recycling center, full of digestive enzymes sealed safely behind a membrane. In Tay-Sachs, one of those enzymes — hexosaminidase A — is missing. Without it, a fatty molecule called GM2 ganglioside can't be broken down, so it accumulates, the lysosome swells, and the cell, especially nerve cells, chokes: muscle weakness, neurological decline, death usually before age three. One enzyme, one compartment, one child's life. When a compartment fails, everything it was holding back comes apart.
